Bubble Up Mechanism & Event Subprocesses in TaktX

General Concept: In BPMN, event subprocesses and the bubble up mechanism are essential for robust error and escalation handling. Event subprocesses are triggered by events (error, escalation, message, timer, etc.) and can interrupt or run in parallel to the main flow. The bubble up mechanism describes how errors and escalations propagate through nested scopes until they are caught by an appropriate handler.

Event Subprocesses in TaktX

Event subprocesses in TaktX are managed on the scope level. When an event occurs, the engine determines the correct scope and starts the event subprocess within that scope. TaktX enforces strict variable scoping, so event subprocesses can access parent variables but can also introduce their own. Event subprocesses can be:

  • Interrupting: Stop the main flow in the scope and start the event subprocess. Used for critical errors or escalations.
  • Non-interrupting: Start the event subprocess in parallel with the main flow. Used for notifications, monitoring, or side effects.

Event subprocesses can be triggered by errors, escalations, messages, timers, or signals. They are powerful for exception handling, compensation, and process recovery.

Error & Escalation Handling and the Bubble Up Mechanism

When an error or escalation is thrown in TaktX, the engine searches for a matching event subprocess or boundary event in the current scope. If not found, the exception "bubbles up" to the parent scope, repeating the search recursively. This continues until the exception is handled or the process instance ends. This mechanism ensures that exceptions are managed according to BPMN semantics, with TaktX-specific enhancements for reliability and clarity.

  • Errors are typically used for unexpected failures. If not caught, they terminate the affected scope and bubble up.
  • Escalations are used for business exceptions or alternative flows. They can be caught by escalation handlers at any level.
  • Both can be caught by event subprocesses or boundary events, either interrupting or non-interrupting.

Variable Scoping in Exception Handling

Each process, subprocess, and event subprocess in TaktX has its own variable scope. Variables are only visible within their scope unless explicitly mapped. When an error or escalation bubbles up, variable cleanup and compensation are handled automatically. This prevents data leaks and ensures process integrity.

Practical Tips for Modeling Robust Processes in TaktX

  • Use interrupting event subprocesses for critical errors that must stop the main flow.
  • Use non-interrupting event subprocesses for monitoring, notifications, or side effects.
  • Always document which errors and escalations can occur and where they are handled.
  • Test your process with both expected and unexpected exceptions to ensure handlers work as intended.
  • Be explicit about variable mappings to avoid accidental data loss or leaks.
  • Use compensation handlers for long-running or transactional activities.

Example: Error Escalation and Bubble Up

Suppose a subprocess throws an error that is not caught locally. The error bubbles up to the parent process, where an interrupting event subprocess catches it and triggers compensation or an alternative flow. If no handler exists, the process instance ends in error. This ensures that all exceptions are either handled or clearly reported.
